6a328739-cacf-4def-8e8b-30a889ab761c.text:
[D3.3 Section 2.1 Methodology]
The design methodology of HYPER-AI architecture is guided by the principles of modularity, scalability and self-management. The overarching aim is to enable the seamless execution of data-intensive applications across the full spectrum of the computing continuum spanning from resource-constrained IoT devices at the edge to high-performance cloud infrastructures.

This section outlines the high-level design principles and the architectural approach adopted to align with the project's vision of an intelligent, hyper-distributed system.

HYPER-AI follows a layered, service-oriented architecture that abstracts resource heterogeneity and promotes interoperability through standardized interfaces and horizontal resource abstractions. Key architectural principles include:

Kubernetes-Native Extension: Kubernetes (K8s)3 is adopted as the core orchestration substrate, extended through Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs), DaemonSets, and dedicated connectors to manage non-container-native devices such as Android Head Mounted Displays (HMDs) and constrained IoT nodes.

8d53bff5-3889-48e2-9772-89bc5e35f8f9.text:
[D3.3 Section 2.1 Methodology]
Computational Resources Abstraction: Resources across all layers (IoT, edge, cloud) are abstracted using the HYPER-AI Resource Model (HRM) to enable uniform access and orchestration, regardless of their native capabilities or interfaces.

Self-CHOP Autonomy: The architecture embeds self-CHOP capabilities, enabling dynamic, autonomous system behavior with minimal human intervention.

DLT-Based Trust and Security: HYPER-AI incorporates distributed ledger technologies (DLTs) to enforce decentralized, zero-trust security models. These include decentralized identity management, distributed access control, audit trails, and tamper-proof data exchange across the computing continuum.

ae4dafd9-9786-4885-8a46-39698df97114.text:
[D3.3 Section 2.1 Methodology]
The architectural framework is explicitly aligned with the conceptual model of the computing continuum, which spans multiple layers of computing from on-device and on-premise deployments to near-edge, far-edge, and centralized cloud infrastructures. The figure below provides a conceptual illustration of this continuum. It captures five representative vertical domains—Manufacturing, Agriculture, Automotive, Energy, and Biotechnology—to showcase how application logic and data processing workflows may span multiple infrastructure layers depending on operational needs.

https://kubernetes.io, Kubernetes Documentation

Figure 1 – HYPER-AI computing continuum landscape

Each vertical presents unique orchestration challenges and heterogeneous infrastructure landscapes. For instance, manufacturing lines may rely on low-latency, on-device intelligence, while national energy systems leverage centralized cloud analytics for large-scale monitoring.

By abstracting these layers under a unified orchestration framework, HYPER-AI enables smart nodes and swarms to be dynamically formed, scaled, and reconfigured based on workload requirements and infrastructure availability.

facdd88f-90b5-4fb1-9dc4-9db6b554e516.text:
[D3.3 Section 2.1 Methodology]
The diagram also highlights the increasing complexity of managing nodes from millions of ultra-low-latency devices on the edge to a few high-capacity nodes in the cloud, with corresponding variations in latency and geographical span. This reinforces the need for distributed intelligence, localized decision-making, and cloud-edge-IoT integration that the HYPER-AI architecture addresses through its generic data models, swarm intelligence mechanisms and adaptive orchestration capabilities.

At the heart of the HYPER-AI computing continuum landscape lies the seamless integration of diverse computational environments including:

IoT Devices and On-Device Nodes: Devices such as sensors, AR glasses, and microcontrollers are integrated via lightweight communication protocols and connectors that translate their capabilities into Kubernetes-compatible descriptors.

Edge Infrastructure: Near and far-edge nodes are equipped with enhanced awareness and resource monitoring capabilities, allowing them to participate in autonomous cluster formation and workload execution.

386523af-ff8c-4959-b137-1e5f49367527.text:
[D3.3 Section 2.1 Methodology]
Cloud Infrastructure: High-performance centralized resources provide additional computing power and storage capacity for tasks requiring global state, deep analytics, or large-scale inference.

2d2477d0-e855-4cab-85e3-da69f2ef52b8.text:
[D4.2 Section 2.1 Open Connectors Overview]
The Open Connectors are a HYPER-AI cloud infrastructure component and is the outcome of Task 4.2 which focuses on the interconnection and management of heterogeneous, multi- modal entities. These entities consist of various computational, storage and network capabilities which form a common Computing Continuum.

The Open Connectors implement a layer of abstraction between the cloud infrastructure and multimodal and diverse edge devices. These edge devices may be (but not limited to) smartphones, XR devices (such as augmented reality equipment, smart glasses) and other devices or computational boards (e.g. Raspberry Pi, GPU-accelerated boards, etc.). These devices do not only form a diverse device group but also combine different OS-bases operated devices (e.g. Linux, Android, etc.). The Open Connectors abstract this multimodality and the diverse characteristics of edge devices and enables the transparent management and interoperability of these edge devices as cloud nodes.

4b14467f-ba1a-41e8-be31-1320415ba37f.text:
[D4.2 Section 2.1 Open Connectors Overview]
The connectors are implemented to create an abstraction layer between the Kubernetes (Kubernetes Documentation, 2025) cloud system and devices that cannot natively execute containers. Therefore, these devices are excluded from being direct Kubernetes nodes and are considered by the HYPER-AI cloud as allocatable resources. The abstraction layer aims to describe these devices in a Kubernetes friendly annotation description to pass them as Kubernetes nodes. The connectors handle the self-advertising and registration (registering the advertised devices as K8s custom resources), the network resources allocation, the network communications required for delegating tasks to the devices (as being nodes of the cluster) and the monitoring of the devices to retain the health of the cluster (as already done with the natively registered K8s worker nodes).

629c301e-2e29-4c96-b756-987b195c366e.text:
[D4.2 Section 2.1 Open Connectors Overview]
The above-mentioned layer of abstraction consists of multiple functionalities which form the framework of the Open Connectors. This framework was deployed in various environments to be developed and tested such as Minikube (Minikube, 2025). The Open Connectors are considered as an internal component of the cloud infrastructure for managing edge devices and schedule applications to these devices. Therefore, they are deployed as deployments and await actions from the edge devices or the cloud users.

All functionalities are also described in a dedicated documentation, existing in the Eclipse GitLab (GitLab Documentation, 2025) repository of the Open Connectors. The first official release version of the connectors is 1.0.0 and implements all the key functionalities expected from T4.2.

964cf0df-6759-4abd-8047-267ab5a13e52.text:
[D4.2 Section 3.1 High Level Architecture]
The HYPER-AI Open Connectors are an open-source project designed to orchestrate and manage edge devices using a Kubernetes-powered control plane. The intended purpose is to implement an abstraction layer between a Kubernetes cluster and resources (Android OS operated smartphones and AR glasses, Containers & Devices) not capable of joining the cluster as native nodes (no support for executing any container runtime).

The Open Connectors are implemented to create an abstraction layer between the Kubernetes cloud system and devices that cannot natively execute containers. The connectors handle the self-advertising and registration (registering the advertised devices as K8s custom resources), the network resources allocation, the network communications required for delegating tasks to the devices (as being nodes of the cluster) and the monitoring of the devices to retain the health of the cluster (as already done with the natively registered K8s worker nodes).

The architecture supports:

• Device registration of self-advertised devices as DeviceNodes.

• Application submission and deployment (to a selected DeviceNode).

• Status tracking and ACK handling.

24aa6461-a069-46dc-bd0f-798836c3cfe8.text:
[D4.2 Section 3.1 High Level Architecture]
• Application submission and deployment (to a selected DeviceNode).

• Status tracking and ACK handling.

• Timeout management for reliability.

The Open Connectors implement the required controllers and communication connectors for enabling devices not capable of joining a K8s cluster natively, as worker nodes in the cluster.

Hence, all nodes are considered as HYPER-AI nodes (following the Data Models implemented on WP4, T4.3) and are categorized into two entities:

Figure 1:Abstraction Entities for Hyper-AI Nodes

12

HYPER-AI | GA: 101135982

The DeviceNode entity is the key descriptor for the edge devices. It is a vital abstraction entity which is used for to correctly provision and delegate tasks to each edge device. The DeviceNode entity consists of specific attributes that describe the edge device’s hardware and software capabilities, including additional sensors operated by the device. The connectors continuously provide each device’s state, resource metrics (e.g. CPU usage), storage utilization, battery reserve, etc.

682bf39f-4bbd-4d98-8b28-c92f643d770a.text:
[D4.2 Section 3.1 High Level Architecture]
The Open Connectors are also responsible for establishing the required communication between the cloud infrastructure, the K8s cluster, and the devices. The devices must maintain communication channels towards the cluster. There are 2 main discrete modules that form the connectors, the Device Controller and the Application Controller. It is important to note that both controllers are directly communicating with the Kubernetes control plane and therefore have elevated access to the cluster’s resources.

66143127-b732-43b3-8ea6-517395029d3c.text:
[D4.2 Section 3.1 High Level Architecture]
The Device Controller is responsible for registering, managing and monitoring every DeviceNode, which in essence is an edge device. Each DeviceNode has a set of attributes that describe its hardware and software capabilities, and attributes dedicated to describing the state of each device. The Device Controller can register new edge devices as DeviceNodes from the self-advertisement of each candidate device (e.g. smartphone, XR glasses). The Device Controller evaluates the advertised device’s information and registers the device as a DeviceNode to Kubernetes. The cluster understands this registration as a new object entry inside the etcd (Etcd, 2020) k8s storage. The controller is also responsible for re-occurringly, patching the DeviceNode’s status attributes with updated values received from each corresponding edge device.

6b7008f1-944f-40ba-af4d-3cc50b4665fb.text:
[D4.2 Section 3.1 High Level Architecture]
The Application Controller is responsible for keeping a record of user-submitted applications targeted for the DeviceNodes. When an application is submitted to the HYPER-AI platform and is intended for a DeviceNode, the Application Controller parses the attributes describing the application (e.g. intended DeviceNode, OS specs, list of required sensors, etc.) and again stores this information in the etcd database. This is mandatory as the scheduler can retrieve this information and the application for scheduling. The controller also monitors the deployment of the application and the execution status.

Each of the controllers implementation consists of the important functionality modules, one for the actual Controller and the other is the Communication Connector. Both of them combined are able to register new edge self-advertised devices as DeviceNodes. This entity is considered as a cloud node, meaning that the specified edge device is set up to be scheduled with tasks for execution and thus, can be considered a cloud node.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This deliverable presents the design, implementation and validation of the softwarized infrastructure and containerization in the form of Open Connectors for the HYPER-AI cloud infrastructure. These Open Connectors are responsible for managing edge devices in the form of cloud-edge resources including edge devices which can be (but not limited to) smartphones and tablets, XR equipment such as smart glasses and any set of devices with different operating systems including among other Linux-based OS and Android. This deliverable, D4.2, documents all the design and implementation aspects of the connectors which form a framework for the registration and management of multimodal edge devices as cloud nodes.

45f0bbbf-36b0-46bc-9704-e612109cc5ab.text:
[D4.2 Executive Summary]
The document begins by describing what the Open Connectors are and what they contribute to the HYPER-AI cloud. An architectural overview of the connectors is described and how there are used as a layer of abstraction between the cloud and heterogeneous and diverse devices as well as how they extend the Kubernetes-native operations and configuration. The open connectors consist of smaller components for registering the edge devices and establishing communication channels towards them. The edge devices, the Device Nodes, are managed by the Open Connectors and are utilized as cloud nodes from the cloud infrastructure.

A detailed description of the development of the Open Connectors is documented in this deliverable to support and explain the design and implementation decisions and methodology applied for implementing all required functionalities. The goal of these connectors is to enable the HYPER-AI cloud infrastructure to manage edge devices as cloud nodes and schedule applications across a cloud-edge-IoT continuum.

0d2e7711-cf6e-4459-b2cb-72de77d75d15.text:
[D4.3 Executive Summary]
This deliverable documents the primary outcomes of Task 4.3 (Open Resources Semantic Representation Models) and Task 4.4 (Application modelling for planning and triggering decision making). The main challenge addressed is the standardisation of application and resource descriptions across a diverse and distributed computing continuum. This is crucial for enabling the automated orchestration, scheduling, and lifecycle management.

The key contributions presented herein are:

1. A Structured, Kubernetes-Native Data Modelling Approach: The project made a strategic decision to move away from formal ontologies (e.g., OWL) towards structured, schema-validated data models using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) and Yet Another Markup Language (YAML). This approach was chosen for its superior performance, simpler integration and reduced architectural complexity.

2. The Application Profile Manager (APM): As the principal outcome of T4.4, the APM is a software stack designed to create, validate, store, query, and update application profiles.

9a24c6da-f710-47ff-9276-3df3d28f72e8.text:
[D4.3 Executive Summary]
It provides a standardised, machine-readable format for describing an application's metadata, resource requirements (CPU, GPU, memory), Quality of Service (QoS) expectations, and deployment constraints. The APM includes a command-line interface (apmctl), a versioned schema registry, and a repository with a representational state transfer (REST) Application Programming Interface (API) for programmatic access.

3. Well-Defined Data Models: This deliverable specifies the data models for both node models and application profiles.

a. Node Models provide a structured description of the capabilities of underlying infrastructure resources, enabling the matching and scheduling logic.

b. Application Profiles are categorised into three types: native for container/ Virtual Machine (VM) workloads, device for hardware-centric edge/IoT applications, and integration for composing multi-component services.

b59bf247-c6e1-46a6-a30f-8f57507676b3.text:
[D4.3 Executive Summary]
4. A Reproducible Workflow: The APM establishes a clear, YAML-first workflow for developers and operators. This process—from initial template generation and schema validation to repository storage and secure API-based updates—ensures that all application descriptors are consistent, valid, and ready for consumption by higher-level orchestration and decision-making components within the HYPER-AI platform.

In conclusion, this deliverable provides the foundational models and tooling necessary for abstracting complex resource capabilities and application needs. The APM and its associated data models are critical inputs for WP5 and WP6, enabling the intelligent and automated management of applications across the HYPER-AI ecosystem.

type: "native"

owner: "UoA-Team"

domain: "education"

specs:

executionType: "container"
entryPoint: "uvicorn"
args: ["main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
baseOS:
name: "python"
version: "3.10-slim"
containerImage:
uri: "nginx"
tag: "latest"

Unlike the spec fields above, status is not set by the user. The platform updates status.phase automatically as the application progresses through its lifecycle:  
| Phase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| pending | Deployment requested, waiting for device ACK |

[IDE Tutorial: Defining Native Applications]
# Defining Native Applications  
A Native Application is described by an application profile — a YAML document with applicationProfile at its root — that defines the workload (container, VM, or binary), its runtime environment, and the requirements that govern where and how it runs.

58086061-82e3-42f5-8a51-09b6f03653c2.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Defining Native Applications > Profile Structure]
## Profile Structure  
Every application profile follows this layout:  
```
applicationProfile:
metadata:
# application identity and annotations
specs:
# runtime, resources, network, constraints, qos
status:
# runtime state, updated dynamically

```  
| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| applicationProfile.metadata | object | ✅ | Application metadata — see metadata |
| applicationProfile.specs | object | ✅ | Application requirements — see the specs sections below |
| applicationProfile.status | object | ❌ | Runtime state, updated dynamically — see status |

672ea38a-3f0d-4a90-9fab-80aa183f77f0.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Hyperion Actions]
# Hyperion Actions  
How your agent talks back to the HyperAI IDE and performs actions.

9ffc9ae5-4e66-471f-b9a6-c9866c58f227.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Hyperion Actions > How it works]
## How it works  
Every time the user types in the Hyperion panel, the IDE sends your agent a
request:  
```
{
"user_id": "3f2a9c11-...",
"text": "Please create a folder for me"
}

```  
- user_id is a UUID generated by the IDE — use it to keep per-user session
memory  
- text is what the user typed.  
Your agent answers with a stream of Server-Sent Events. Each event is a
data: line holding one JSON object, followed by a blank line. There are two
kinds of event, and the IDE treats them very differently.

8627a1b0-692c-4731-9fa0-16299062dbc6.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Hyperion Actions > Streaming text]
## Streaming text  
Anything you stream as response shows up in the Hyperion panel as the
assistant's message:  
```
data: {"response": "Creating the folder "}

data: {"response": "for you."}

```  
Each chunk is an increment, not the whole message — the IDE appends them
one after the other, which is what produces the typing effect. The message is
complete when your response body closes.

f9edea83-2bd9-4213-9cd3-b0a1db9960c1.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Hyperion Actions > Sending an action]
## Sending an action  
When you want the agent to actually do something in the IDE, stream an event
with an action key instead of the response key used for
streaming text:  
```
data: {"action": "create_folder", "path": "demo/sub"}

```  
The IDE executes it and prints nothing for it. If you want to tell the user
what the action did, you have to stream that text yourself as response
events (see Streaming text):  
```
data: {"response": "I'll create the folder "}

data: {"response": "`demo/sub` for you."}

data: {"action": "create_folder", "path": "demo/sub"}

data: {"response": " Done — you can see it in the file explorer."}

```  
Actions and text can come in any order, and you can send several actions in one
answer.

17bb4686-539c-4fc0-9e59-8800cab2eb55.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Hyperion Actions > Available actions]
## Available actions  
| Action | Payload | What the IDE does | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| create_folder | path | Creates the folder. | {"action":"create_folder","path":"demo/sub"} |
| delete_folder | path | Deletes the folder. | {"action":"delete_folder","path":"demo"} |
| create_file | path, content | Creates the file and opens it in the editor. | {"action":"create_file","path":"demo/nginx.yaml","content":"apiVersion: hyper.ai/v1\n..."} |
| edit_file | path, content | Finds the file and replaces it whole, then opens it in the editor. | {"action":"edit_file","path":"nginx.yaml","content":"apiVersion: hyper.ai/v1\n..."} |
| delete_file | path | Deletes the file. | {"action":"delete_file","path":"nginx.yaml"} |  
path is always relative to the workspace root — never absolute, never ...  
For delete_file, edit_file and delete_folder you do not need to give the
whole path — send just the name and the IDE searches the workspace and uses the
first match. If you do specify a path, it is taken into account and used
as-is.

3cd85dd3-9f58-4ba8-bc6c-cf64a27fcea6.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Hyperion Actions > Reading a file — the read_file helper]
## Reading a file — the read_file helper  
Reading a file is deliberately not an action. To see what is inside a file, your agent asks the
IDE backend directly over HTTP.  
The starter ships that call as a helper in helpers.py:  
```
from helpers import read_file

content = await read_file("app.yaml")

```  
It returns the file as a plain string.  
- The path argument is either a full path (demo/sub/app.yaml) or just a
file name. Send only the name and the backend searches the whole workspace
for it, the same way delete_file does.  
Errors  
On failure it raises ReadFileError. Possible causes are several files share that
name (all of them listed, so you can ask the user which one), or the backend
is unreachable.  
Under the hood read_file is one GET against the IDE backend:  
```
GET http://localhost:3001/api/agent/file?path=app.yaml
GET http://localhost:3001/api/agent/file?path=demo/app.yaml

metadata.section: Reading a file — the read_file helper

2d6103a6-34cf-4733-8b1d-3c53b9e2afb1.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Hyperion Actions > Reading a file — the read_file helper]
```  
Slashes are allowed as-is in the query string, so a full path needs no
special treatment (demo%2Fapp.yaml is accepted too).  
| Status | Body |
|---|---|
| 200 | {"path": "demo/sub/app.yaml", "content": "..."} — path is where it actually lives |
| 404 | {"error": "File not found"} |
| 409 | {"error": "Ambiguous file name", "matches": [...]} |

metadata.section: Reading a file — the read_file helper

924086df-54d5-4679-b0a9-62fb51447fa9.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Hyperion Actions > Validating a file — the validate_file helper]
## Validating a file — the validate_file helper  
Validating is not an action either. Your agent asks the IDE backend to check
a file against the Native Apps or Device Apps
rules. You send only the path — the backend reads the file itself.  
```
from helpers import validate_file

report = await validate_file("app.yaml")

```  
It returns the report as a dict:  
```
{
"path": "demo/app.yaml",
"type": "device",
"valid": false,
"errors": [
{"line": 3, "column": 1, "endLine": 3, "endColumn": 9, "field": "metadata.name", "message": "is required"}
],
"warnings": [
{"line": 12, "column": 5, "endLine": 12, "endColumn": 12, "field": "spec.exec.retries", "message": "unknown field, not part of the schema"}
]
}

metadata.section: Validating a file — the validate_file helper

48bb9fc0-3988-4e1f-969b-41a752ef54ce.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Hyperion Actions > Validating a file — the validate_file helper]
```  
- type is native or device.  
- valid is false as soon as there is one error.  
- line and column point at the problem. For a missing field they point at
the section where it should be added.  
The path works the same way as
in read_file — a full path or just a
name.  
Errors  
On failure it raises ValidateFileError, for the same reasons as
read_file. An invalid file is not an error — you get the report with
valid: false.  
Under the hood validate_file is one GET against the IDE backend:  
```
GET http://localhost:3001/api/agent/validation/file?path=app.yaml

```  
| Status | Body |
|---|---|
| 200 | the report |
| 404 | {"error": "File not found"} |
| 409 | {"error": "Ambiguous file name", "matches": [...]} |  
Local vs Docker  
If you have followed the challenge description, then when you run the
agent locally the ide-backend is at http://localhost:3001/api. When
the agent runs as a Docker container, the backend must be
http://host.docker.internal:3001/api instead.  
In the hyperion-starter
this is already set in the Dockerfile, so nothing to change:  
```
git clone https://gitlab.eclipse.org/eclipse-research-labs/hyper-ai-project/hyperion-starter.git

```

metadata.section: Validating a file — the validate_file helper

7f15b848-e5bd-48e2-9909-c9afd99cb242.text:
[IDE Tutorial: IDE Guide > Login / Signup]
## Login / Signup  
Opening the IDE redirects you to the HyperAI sign-in page. Enter your email and password and click Sign In. New users can create an account through the Register link, and Forgot Password? starts a reset.

2efab06b-2894-4b5f-80af-1b00078c6f9f.text:
[IDE Tutorial: IDE Guide > Using the Wizard]
## Using the Wizard  
The Wizard is a smart way to define your application in an easy way. Open it by clicking New App Profile in the top bar.  
You can either fill in the form or edit the Wizard DSL in the mini editor — the two stay in sync, and validation errors are shown live.  
When you finalize, click Generate YAML — the YAML is automatically sent to the main YAML editor.

bbdafa08-263a-45c6-8816-1c23a6632b93.text:
[IDE Tutorial: IDE Guide > Settings]
## Settings  
To customize the IDE, click Settings in the top bar. From there you can change the theme, the font size, and many more — or reset everything back to the defaults with Reset Defaults.

f36f83b1-ed0f-4a44-b47a-ef62dccf829e.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Introduction > About HyperAI]
## About HyperAI  
The demand for efficient data processing has surged in modern computing.
However, traditional infrastructures face challenges in meeting the intensive
requirements of diverse applications, from complex simulations to real-time
analytics. What complicates matters is the varied nature of computing resources
across the Cloud, Edge, and IoT domains, each presenting unique challenges and
opportunities.  
In this context, the EU-funded HYPER-AI project aims to redefine data
processing by harnessing distributed computing swarms. These are autonomous
networks of interconnected nodes that dynamically adapt and optimise resources
throughout the computing continuum. By implementing semantic representation
and autonomic principles, HYPER-AI promises enhanced self-configuring,
self-healing, and self-optimising capabilities.  
Visit the project website at hyper-ai-project.eu
for more information about the consortium, objectives, and outputs.

0e78ef20-026e-4207-8cbd-0b4ef3f46c3d.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Quick Start Demo]
# Quick Start Demo  
Deploy your first web server on HyperAI with a few simple steps.  
Open the IDE at ide.hyperai.di.uoa.gr and follow along.

f39c27d9-40a1-41c5-a51c-d96f7249a540.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Quick Start Demo > Step 0 — Publish your image to a whitelisted registry]
## Step 0 — Publish your image to a whitelisted registry  
Before deploying, your container must live in a public registry whitelisted by HyperAI — for example Docker Hub. You'll reference it in Step 3 when building your Application Profile.  
Build the image locally:  
```
docker build -t <user>/<image>:<tag> .

```  
Push it to the registry:  
```
docker push <user>/<image>:<tag>

```  
Further reading  
Follow the official Docker Hub quickstart for more information.

metadata.section: Step 0 — Publish your image to a whitelisted registry

4baea1c3-5750-4aaa-9da3-5dc767d7e986.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Quick Start Demo > Step 1 — Sign in]
## Step 1 — Sign in  
When you open the IDE you are redirected to the HyperAI sign-in page. Enter your email and password and click Sign In.  
If you don't have an account yet, click Register and create one first.

541a4c3b-b0a0-4c07-81ab-ed9b0a5e874d.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Quick Start Demo > Step 2 — Create a working directory for your app]
## Step 2 — Create a working directory for your app  
You can create a working directory for organizing your app, or group of apps. This is done through the Workspace Explorer by clicking Create Folder.

metadata.section: Step 2 — Create a working directory for your app

b3e5ef35-a260-466f-ad31-8becd3d9e5f8.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Quick Start Demo > Step 3 — Create your Application Profile .yaml]
## Step 3 — Create your Application Profile .yaml  
After creating the working directory, the application profile .yaml document must be created. Application profiles contain all the attributes of the app the user wants to run. Again this is done through the Workspace Explorer by clicking Create File. Name the file accordingly and add .yaml at the end.  
To build the profile, consult the DSL Specification: Native Apps for native applications, or Device Apps for applications meant to run on a device. You can also find ready-to-use examples in the Cookbook & Examples. This is where you reference the container image you pushed in Step 0.

5e9b315a-99ae-408e-9071-d9c66b944b3b.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Quick Start Demo > Step 4 — Deployment]
## Step 4 — Deployment  
When you are ready, click the Deploy button. Before this step, make sure each profile has been saved.  
In the popup window, select the workflow you want to deploy and click Deploy. Multiple profiles can be deployed at the same time.  
You will be asked to manually change the workflow name — if you don't want to, just skip it by clicking OK.

151bd11f-9618-412d-b1a2-aa12963f1a6a.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Quick Start Demo > Step 5 — Start your workflows]
## Step 5 — Start your workflows  
If you haven't received an error message, click the Dashboard. In the list of deployments, find the one you just deployed and press Start.  
This may take some time until the workflow status is Running.

a5207ad7-2b2a-4210-ba15-c1110ab2e927.text:
[IDE Tutorial: Quick Start Demo > Tips]
## Tips  
If you want to see live analytics of your workflow, click the Metrics button.
